planting.note: Divide clumps in spring and plant into cool, consistently moist soil near a pond or stream edge; lowland gardens need reliable irrigation and some afternoon shade to avoid heat stress.

directions: A subalpine snowmelt-meadow sedge, this species wants the opposite treatment from typical dry-shade sedges: constant soil moisture, cool root zones, and a real winter chill. Its dense clumps and dark-purplish nodding flower spikes suit a cool, moist rock garden or alpine-style planting where snow lingers into spring. In lowland gardens outside its natural elevation band, give it reliable irrigation and afternoon shade to compensate for summer heat it would never experience at altitude.

planting.note: Divide the mounding tussock in spring and root into a rocky or gravelly substrate at a stream edge; tolerates seasonal flooding and scouring once established.

directions: In the wild this sedge roots directly into rock crevices along creeks, forming a striking fountain-shaped mounding tussock unusually tolerant of winter inundation and scouring flows for a garden sedge. Give it a rocky or gravelly substrate rather than rich loam, keep it moist through summer, and it forms a dense, low-maintenance mound within two to three years. It is one of the best true boulder-and-stream sedges for a naturalistic water feature where ordinary garden Carex would rot.

planting.note: Divide clumps in fall and plant into dry, well-drained duff beneath oaks or in chaparral soil; avoid regular summer irrigation, which causes rot in this dry-adapted species.

directions: Unlike most shade sedges that demand moisture, this fine-textured, reed-like species specifically wants dry, well-drained shade — the duff layer beneath oaks or chaparral shrubs rather than a bog or rain garden. It makes a good low-water companion for manzanita and ceanothus plantings where other Carex would fail from root rot in dry-summer gardens. Leave it undisturbed once established, since it is slow to recover from transplant shock.

planting.note: Divide rhizomatous clumps in spring and plant into a partial-shade rain garden or seasonal-seep simulation with moderate to consistent moisture.

directions: Native to seeps and spring-fed hillsides across a wide range of California plant communities, from coastal prairie to foothill woodland, this rhizomatous sedge tolerates more variability in light and soil moisture than strict wetland species. That flexibility makes it a good choice for a partial-shade rain garden or a simulated seasonal seep rather than a permanently flooded bed. Pair it with Carex nudata or other streamside sedges for a layered planting of varying heights and textures.

planting.note: Divide rhizome sections in spring and plant into consistently saturated soil at a pond margin or wet forest understory where its assertive spread is welcome.

directions: One of the largest western native Carex, this species carries blue-green leaves and showy seed heads on a genuinely architectural scale, making it a strong vertical accent for pond edges and bioswales. It spreads with real vigor by rhizome in saturated soil, so site it where that spread is wanted — wet forest understory restoration or a pond margin — rather than a tight border bed. Reddish stem bases and wide, roughly hairy leaves give it textural interest other wetland sedges lack.

planting.note: Divide loose tussocks in spring and plant into the lowest, soggiest point of a rain garden or pond margin where soil stays saturated or seasonally submerged.

directions: This true 'wet feet' sedge carries attractive lime-green seed heads and genuinely wants to sink its roots into muck rather than merely moist soil, making it well suited to the lowest, soggiest points of a rain garden or pond margin where other ornamentals fail. Its loose, sparse tussocks colonize gradually into dense stands over a few seasons. It is one of the few West Coast native sedges commonly sold as restoration seed rather than nursery plugs, so a meadowscape or pond-margin seed mix is a practical source.

planting.note: Divide small clumps in spring and plant into open sun or very light shade with sharp drainage; this species is shade-intolerant and declines if overtopped by taller vegetation or planted in heavy soil.

directions: Despite a diminutive habit that might suggest a shade groundcover, this species actually needs open sun or only very light shade and sharp drainage, declining quickly in deep shade or heavy clay. It forms a dense, low, fine-textured clump with excellent drought tolerance once established, fitting naturally into a dry-garden planting alongside sagebrush, bitterbrush, or open ponderosa pine understory. Treat it as a short-statured dry-garden groundcover rather than a woodland-shade sedge.
sources: US Forest Service Fire Effects Information System (FEIS)

planting.note: Divide and plant at higher density than typical for Carex, since this species is notoriously slow to establish from either seed or division; site in dry, well-drained pine or fir understory.

directions: The signature dry-montane-forest-floor sedge of the Interior West, this species is an ecologically important drought-tolerant groundcover and critical wildlife forage, but it is also horticulturally patient — slow to establish and not a fast-filling lawn alternative. Plant at higher density than usual and expect several years before it forms a solid colony in dry pine or fir understory. It needs only modest annual precipitation and tolerates genuinely cold winters once established.
sources: US Forest Service Fire Effects Information System (FEIS)

planting.note: Divide rhizome sections in spring and plant with ample room in a large rain-garden basin or along an eroding wet bank; colonizes aggressively once established.

directions: A robust, widely adaptable rhizomatous wetland sedge with soft, woolly-haired seed heads, this species is a workhorse for wet-meadow restoration, pond margins, and erosion control on wet banks across sand, loam, silt, or gravel soils. It colonizes aggressively by rhizomes in consistently wet soil, so give it room rather than treating it as a tidy clumper. Its range reaches well into the Rocky Mountain states, making it a legitimate continental wetland sedge rather than a strict regional endemic.

planting.note: Divide clumps in spring and plant into a bioswale or rain garden receiving road runoff or hard, alkaline water, where this species outperforms most other sedges.

directions: A premier western wetland sedge with waxy blue-green foliage, this species stands out for its exceptional tolerance of alkaline and saline soils and periodic submersion, succeeding where other sedges struggle. It tolerates sand, loam, or clay and even prolonged submersion, making it very forgiving for pond-margin plantings across the Intermountain West and California. It is a strong choice specifically for bioswales or rain gardens with hard or alkaline water.
